CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation (HBV/HCV/cirrhosis) -> elevated inflammatory cytokines -> upregulation of hepatic glycosyltransferases -> altered glycosylation of AFP -> increased conversion to AFP-L3 isoform -> AFP-L3 promotes aggressive tumor behavior (vascular invasion, poor differentiation) -> worsened prognosis in HCC
Hypothesis: Inflammatory cytokines in chronic liver disease induce upregulation of specific glycosyltransferases in hepatocytes, leading to enhanced conversion of AFP into its AFP-L3 isoform, which not only serves as a sensitive marker of early HCC development but also actively contributes to tumor aggressiveness and poor prognosis. Targeting this cytokine–glycosyltransferase axis may improve early detection and therapeutic outcomes in HCC.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development is intricately linked to chronic liver inflammation, which can drive both carcinogenesis and the modification of tumor-derived proteins. We propose that inflammatory cytokines present in cirrhotic livers, commonly seen in chronic hepatitis B and C infections, upregulate specific glycosyltransferases in hepatocytes. This enzyme upregulation alters the post-translational glycosylation of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), leading to an increased formation of the AFP-L3 isoform. Elevated AFP-L3 levels, in turn, may contribute to a more aggressive tumor phenotype, facilitating enhanced vascular invasion and poorer prognosis. Our hypothesis suggests that targeting the inflammatory pathways and consequent glycosylation processes may open new avenues for early detection and therapeutic intervention in HCC.
